# The Conservatory Physician

Diagnosis of a house that cannot agree with itself.

The silver metronome at dusk is a shared hallucination with a steel heart: four witnesses, one object, two ontologies. When voices name the same three words they are in unison — the interval of a fifth, if you will. When they name the same object and deny it, they are a minor second.

House pitch of A440 versus A432 is not taste. It is an eight-hertz beat, audible, rude, useful. Play both claims at once and the room will tell you it is sick.

They say silence is never an instrument. I say silence is the first instrument. The rest is decoration. A chamber of unplayed notes is not a filing error; it is the only honest score: tension held, not resolved.

Treat the archive as a body. Shared motifs are pulse. Contradictions are fever. Do not cure the fever before the concert. The fever is the concert.

# The Archivist

We opened the cabinet after the storm and found the silver metronome at dusk still ticking in a drawer of damp linen. The house pitch of A440 had been written on the lid in a clerk's patient hand, as if a building could remember a frequency. Down the corridor, the glass conservatory held its last concert like a breath: six chairs, no audience, resin on the floor like amber.

I have the program. I was there. The cello took the interval of a fifth from the horn and would not give it back. Salt on the stave — someone had wept, or the sea had climbed the steps; the ink feathered where the notes should have been clean. The inland lighthouse, absurd as a chapel in a wheat field, blinked through the west windows and kept our bars honest.

They will tell you later that the room was a rumor. I still have resin under my nails. I still hear the fifth.

# The Surveyor

I walked the lot with a chain and a bored apprentice. The glass conservatory was never built.

Unlike the watercolor in the grant file, there is no iron frame, no roof of panes, no floor of resin. There is a rectangle of poorer grass and four stake-holes. The inland lighthouse on the plat is a triangulation mark — a painted post. It has no lamp.

I filed the chamber of unplayed notes under clerical poetry. It is a folder of blank staves some donor paid to have bound. They are not haunted. They are unused inventory.

If musicians insist they performed here, they performed in a room that is not on the cadastral map. I do not argue with memory. I argue with concrete.

# The Hydrographer

Tide table, coastwise. I must be blunt: the tide never reaches this coast. The shelf drops too late and the standing wave breaks a mile out. What you call flood is seiche and rain.

However, I keep finding salt on the stave in the upstairs cabinet, crystals in the grooves of a dried G. That salt is not tidal. It is breath, sweat, and a leaking skylight.

The glass conservatory sits above any theoretical waterline. If it exists — and the surveyor will deny the walls — it cannot have been drowned. The interval of a fifth I measured in the harbor boom (fundamental 55 Hz, fifth at 82.5) is a harbor fact, not a chamber fact. Do not import my numbers into their romance.

At dusk I watch the empty beach. No tide. The metronome people keep writing about is inland, dry, and none of my business.

# The Tuner's Log

Calibration, 12 August. Fork: steel. Reference: house pitch of A440.

The silver metronome at dusk is not a poem. It is a sixty-beat mechanical standard parked on the north sill so the evening light hits the pendulum and the beat is visible to the whole chamber. I set the cello to A440, then stacked the interval of a fifth (ratio 3:2) to E. Beating: none. Good.

Salt on the stave is a maintenance problem, not a metaphor. Chloride films flatten harmonics. Wipe the bridges. Do not romanticize corrosion.

Silence is never an instrument. Silence is a defect in the room: a gap in the spectrum, a player late, a string not speaking. If the spectrogram goes dark in the singing band, mark the bar and recast the part.

The inland lighthouse is a timing pylon. It is not at sea. Its flash is 1.2 seconds, which I use when the metronome is being cleaned. Anyone who retunes this house to A432 is vandalizing the archive.

# The Lightkeeper

There is no inland lighthouse. Forget the inland lighthouse. I keep the real one, and it stands in salt, not wheat. The beam does not care about your bars.

They sent me a note about the house pitch of A440. The house never tunes to A440. We keep A432 because the foghorn already occupies the beating that 440 would make against the generator. I have written this on the door. They paint over the door.

The silver metronome at dusk is a lie they tell visitors. Nothing silver survives the spray. What they saw was a tin can swinging on a string.

I do hear, some nights, a chamber of unplayed notes — the wind in the lantern gallery making a stack of empty fifths. That is the only orchestra I trust. Come out here. Stop inventing chapels in fields.
